meta.blurb: Maya is always rushing, always somewhere else in her head. Over six weeks of small, honest practice, she learns to arrive in her own life, one breath at a time. A calm, practical guide to being here.
meta.bible: Maya Ellis: a busy office worker of about thirty, always rushing and checking her phone. Mrs Adeyemi: the calm, kind teacher of the Thursday evening class at the Community hall. Joe: Maya's colleague, friendly and a little careless with emails. Maya's mother: visits one weekend. Nia: Maya's young niece. The story takes place in an ordinary town over about Six weeks, from one Monday to a final Thursday. Key terms: Mindfulness, Autopilot, Anchor, Breath, Body scan, Present moment, Weather, Wave, Pause. Mindfulness practice has roots in Buddhist teaching about two and a half thousand years old, and is taught today in religious and non-religious ways. The science is hedged: studies suggest it helps many people with stress, but not everyone, and it is not a cure. Voice and tone: warm, calm, concrete and honest; one clear idea in each beat; no claims that anything fixes everything; Mrs Adeyemi never preaches. Beat 50 reminds the reader that this book is general information and that anyone who feels very low or anxious for a long time should speak to a doctor.

C1C2: On Monday morning Maya stood in her kitchen reading messages while the toast turned black and the smoke alarm began to shout. She grabbed her bag and sprinted for the corner, only to watch the bus pull away from the stop. It was the third time that month, and she could not remember when she had last done anything without hurrying.

The later bus carried Maya through half the town while her eyes stayed fixed on a screen full of small, urgent things. When she finally looked up, she realised that she could not recall a single street, shop or face from the whole journey. Her body had been present, yet her mind had been somewhere else entirely, which is a thing that happens to most of us every day.

When Joe asked a simple question about a report, Maya answered so sharply that he stepped back from her desk with a hurt look. She felt ashamed almost at once, but the words had already left her mouth and could not be called back. Too tired and too busy to notice her own mood, she had let it speak for her.

On the way home, Maya noticed a hand-painted poster on the wall of the Community hall, offering a gentle Thursday evening class called Be Here. She would normally have hurried past without a glance, but that evening something in her tired mind said stop. Before she could argue herself out of it, she had written the time on her hand.

Mrs Adeyemi, a calm woman with a soft voice and unhurried hands, greeted every person in the circle by name and invited them to sit. She told the class that nobody was broken and nothing needed to be fixed, and that the only task was to practise being where they were. Maya, who had arrived expecting to be told what she was doing wrong, felt her shoulders loosen a little.

For the first exercise, Mrs Adeyemi asked everyone to rest both feet on the floor and simply feel them for one whole minute. Maya managed perhaps five seconds before her thoughts leapt ahead to tomorrow's meeting, then to the shopping, then to a conversation from last week. It was the longest minute she could remember, and she was surprised by how hard such a small task could be.

The mind, Mrs Adeyemi explained, is a restless traveller that spends most of its time in yesterday or tomorrow. We replay old conversations, rehearse future ones and worry about things that may never happen, while the only moment we can actually live slips quietly past. None of this is a fault, she added, because planning and remembering are useful, but it helps to know when we are doing it.

Many people expect the present moment to feel dramatic, but Mrs Adeyemi told the class that it is nearly always small and ordinary. It might be a cup of tea going cold, the hum of a refrigerator or the weight of your own hands on your knees. Its quietness is exactly what makes it a reliable place for a restless mind to return to.

To give the wandering mind somewhere to rest, Mrs Adeyemi suggested the breath, which she called an anchor. It is always with us, it asks for no equipment, and it can only ever happen in this moment, never in the past or the future. Maya laid a hand on her chest and felt, for the first time in years, the slow tide of her own breathing.

Maya closed her eyes and began to count her breaths, determined to reach ten without a single slip. She got as far as three before she found herself deep in a thoughtful debate about pasta or rice for dinner. She opened her eyes, certain that she had failed, but Mrs Adeyemi was smiling at her.

A wandering mind is not a failure, Mrs Adeyemi told her, because minds wander just as hearts beat and rivers run. The real skill lies in the moment you notice that you have drifted, for that small moment of waking up is the practice itself. Each time you notice, she said, you are strengthening something, even if it feels like you are only starting over.

When you bring your attention back, Mrs Adeyemi advised, do it as a kind teacher guides a young child back to her desk after a wander round the room. There is no scolding in it and no sigh of disappointment, only a patient hand and a friendly voice. The tone you use inwardly matters just as much as the returning itself, she said.

The homework for the week was modest, and Mrs Adeyemi promised that it would be enough: five minutes of sitting each morning, with attention resting on the breath. Maya set a timer on her phone, feeling oddly shy about it, as though she were hiding a small secret from the rest of her busy life. She decided to begin the very next day, before the morning could get ahead of her.

By the third morning, five minutes felt as long as a rainy afternoon, and a sudden itch appeared on the side of Maya's nose. Remembering Mrs Adeyemi's advice, she decided to watch it rather than scratch it, and she noticed how it pulsed, grew sharper and then quietly faded away. It was a small discovery, but it taught her that even uncomfortable feelings do not last for ever.

In the fourth class, everyone lay on a mat while Mrs Adeyemi guided their attention slowly from the toes up through the legs, the back and the arms to the top of the head. At each place they were asked only to notice what was there, whether warmth, tingling, tension or nothing at all. Maya was astonished by how many parts of her body she had ignored for years.

Halfway up her back, Maya fell fast asleep and began to snore very softly, to her own great embarrassment when she woke. Mrs Adeyemi only laughed kindly and said that this happens often, because most of us are carrying more tiredness than we realise. Sleep is not a sin, she added, but in the practice we try to stay gently awake.

For five whole minutes the class simply listened, letting sounds arrive without naming them or deciding whether they were pleasant. Maya heard the rain on the glass, the hum of a heater and a distant siren, and she noticed that each sound came, stayed a little while and went. Hearing, she realised, asks nothing of us except that we stay present and let the world come in.

The next morning, Maya left her phone in her bag and let the bus fill her ears instead of her eyes. She heard two friends laughing about a film, a toddler humming a half-remembered song and the soft sigh of the doors, all of which had been there on every journey she had ever taken. It felt like finding a door in a house she had lived in for years.

At lunchtime, Maya set her phone face down on the desk and ate her soup one spoonful at a time, as if she were meeting it for the first time. She noticed the warmth of the bowl, the sharpness of the pepper and a sweet note of carrot that she had never really tasted before. She was still hungry for a second helping afterwards, but it felt like a pleasant kind of hunger.

Sitting at her desk before a deadline, Maya did what Mrs Adeyemi had asked and checked in with her body from top to bottom. Her shoulders had crept up towards her ears, her jaw was clenched like a fist and her breath was high and shallow in her chest. Stress, she discovered, announces itself in the body long before the mind admits it.

An email arrived from Joe that began with a cheerful greeting and ended with an unfair complaint, and Maya's fingers were already on the keys before she had finished reading. Then she remembered the pause, took one slow breath and felt her heartbeat settle a little. That tiny gap was enough to let her see that she had a choice.

Maya wrote a short and friendly reply that explained the problem without blaming anyone, and she pressed send before the old irritation could return. A few minutes later Joe appeared at her desk with a sheepish grin and apologised for his careless message. It had cost her only one breath, and it had saved them both an afternoon of tension.

Our feelings, Mrs Adeyemi told the class, are a little like weather: they arrive without asking, they change without warning, and they always pass. You cannot order the rain to stop, but you can learn to stand in it without believing you are the storm. The sky behind every cloud, she said, is the part of us that stays.

Before her first big presentation, a fluttering started in Maya's stomach and spread upwards until her hands were trembling around her notes. Instead of fighting the feeling, she silently gave it a name and said to herself that worry was here, which made it seem less like a flood and more like a visitor. She was still afraid, but for the first time in her life she was not afraid of being afraid.

Maya admitted that she had always thought acceptance meant giving up, and she asked Mrs Adeyemi whether she was supposed to simply put up with everything. Mrs Adeyemi shook her head and explained that acceptance only means seeing clearly what is true at this moment, whether you like it or not. From that honest place, she said, you can decide calmly what to do next.

The thought I will mess this up, Mrs Adeyemi pointed out, can feel as solid as a wall, yet it is only a sentence passing through the mind. It describes a fear and not a fact, and it has no power to predict what will happen tomorrow. Learning to see thoughts as thoughts is a bit like learning to see clouds as clouds.

When her name was called, Maya stood, felt both feet on the floor and let one slow breath leave her body before she spoke. Her voice shook a little at the start, but it steadied as she found her place, and she noticed that the fear was still there beside her without taking over. It was not a perfect talk, yet it was an honest one, and the room clapped.

Mrs Adeyemi was careful never to promise too much, and that week she reminded the class that this practice will not make problems disappear. Studies suggest that it helps many people manage stress, though not everyone, and researchers still debate how much of the benefit comes from the practice itself. It is best treated, she said, as a useful skill and not a miracle.

The queue at the supermarket stretched all the way back to the bread, and the old Maya would have sighed, tapped her foot and scrolled through her phone. Instead she felt the ground under her shoes, followed the rise and fall of her breath and looked around at the faces with curiosity. Waiting, she noticed, was only time, and for once it felt like her own time to use.

At dinner with a friend, Maya felt a sharp pull towards the phone in her bag, as familiar as an itch. She sat still and watched the urge swell, reach a peak and then roll slowly away, exactly as Mrs Adeyemi had described. When it was gone, she realised that she had been listening to her friend with both ears for the first time all evening.

When her mother came to stay for the weekend, Maya set her phone in a drawer and gave her undivided attention to every story, even the ones she had heard a dozen times. Her mother paused halfway through a tale about the neighbour's garden and said, with surprise, that Maya seemed different. Maya only smiled to herself and reached for the teapot, because she knew exactly why that was so.

Full attention, Mrs Adeyemi told the class, may be the most generous gift we can give another person. Most of us listen while quietly preparing our reply, so that we are only half present, whereas real listening means hearing the whole sentence and letting the answer arrive on its own. People can usually feel the difference at once, even if they cannot say what it is.

A customer in the shop where Maya sometimes helped on Saturdays shouted at her about a late order, and she felt heat climb up her neck. She noticed it, took a slow breath and chose her words carefully instead of snapping back as she once would have. The man did not become pleasant, but the conversation ended without anger, and she walked home feeling quietly proud.

On her way to the station, Maya decided to walk as though the pavement were worth knowing, feeling the heel meet the ground, the push of the toes and the cool air against her cheeks. Morning light slanted through the trees in long gold bars, and she wondered how many hundreds of mornings she had walked beneath them without looking up. The journey took exactly the same time as always, but it felt twice as full.

Small pleasures began to appear in Maya's days like stars coming out at dusk: steam curling from her tea, a patch of sunlight sliding across the wall, the smell of bread from the bakery on the corner. They had been there all along, patiently waiting for her to arrive and to notice them. Happiness, she began to suspect, is less often something we chase than something we overlook.

After a hectic week, Maya missed four mornings in a row and arrived at class convinced that she had ruined everything. Mrs Adeyemi was not at all disturbed and told her that there is no score in this practice, only the next moment in which she can begin again. Starting over, she said, is not a punishment but the very heart of the whole thing.

Maya had a harsh critic living in her head, one that called her lazy and hopeless whenever she missed a morning. Mrs Adeyemi asked her to imagine saying those same words to a close friend, and Maya was shocked at how cruel they sounded. From then on she tried to answer herself the way she would answer someone she loved.

Maya had been waiting for a perfect corner, a perfect cushion and a perfectly quiet hour, and so she had often not practised at all. Mrs Adeyemi laughed and told her that an ordinary chair would do, adding that a few minutes of regular practice are worth more than one long session every now and then. The best time to start, she said, is usually the one you already have.

Mindfulness, Mrs Adeyemi told the class, has its roots in Buddhist teaching that is about two and a half thousand years old, although today it is also taught in schools and clinics without any religion attached. Many other traditions have their own ways of quiet attention, such as prayer, contemplation and silent walking, and she encouraged each person to respect whatever path felt right to them. The practice belongs to everyone, she said, and to no single group, and it asks only that you take it with respect.

One night Maya lay awake long after midnight, watching the shadow of a streetlight crawl across the ceiling, and her old habit was to argue with the darkness. This time she felt the weight of her body on the mattress and followed her breath, with no promise that sleep would come. It did not come at once, but the night felt gentler, and the frustration loosened its grip.

One afternoon Joe leaned on the edge of her desk and asked, in his usual easy way, what had changed, because she seemed so much calmer. Maya told him about the Thursday class in plain, modest words, taking care not to make it sound like magic or a cure. He listened closely, nodded and then asked her for the address of the hall.

Instead of juggling ten tasks and a buzzing phone, Maya began to do one thing at a time, closing every other window on her screen. The report took about as long as it always had, but she finished it without the usual jittery exhaustion and with fewer silly mistakes. Doing one thing fully, she discovered, can be more restful than doing many things badly.

One morning Maya knocked her coffee across the whole table, and she felt the familiar heat of self-blame begin to rise within her. She noticed it with mild interest, as one might notice a light turning red, and found herself laughing instead of cursing. Clearing it up took thirty seconds, and the day simply went on, a little lighter than before.

On the anniversary of her grandmother's death, a deep sadness settled over Maya like fog, and for once she did not try to push it away or distract herself. She sat with it kindly, letting it be as large as it needed to be, and found that it softened a little as the hours went by. Mrs Adeyemi had been clear that very heavy feelings call for other people, such as friends or a doctor, and that asking for help is a strength.

It rained on the Saturday of Maya's long-planned picnic, and disappointment struck her like a small slammed door. She let herself feel it for a minute, and then she noticed the smell of wet grass, the silver patter of drops on the leaves and the strange gold light behind the clouds. The day was not the one she had planned, but it was a real day all the same.

On the last Thursday, the class sat in their circle once more, and Mrs Adeyemi thanked each person for the honesty and courage they had brought. There would be no certificate, she said with a twinkle, because this is not something that you finish, only something that you carry with you from one ordinary day to the next. Maya felt a small ache of gratitude as she put on her coat and walked out into the evening.

Six weeks after the burned toast, Maya stood in the very same kitchen, in the very same dressing gown, and watched her bread turn slowly golden. Nothing in the room had changed, yet everything felt different, because this time she was actually there to see it. She caught the toast just in time and sat down to eat it without her phone.

It would be a lie to say that Maya had become a perfectly peaceful person, because some days she still rushed, worried and checked her phone far too often. The difference was that she now noticed it sooner, sometimes within seconds, and could come gently back to her breath and her feet. She had not escaped from her mind, only learned to live with it more kindly.

When her small niece Nia burst into tears over a broken toy, Maya knelt beside her and showed her how to feel her feet on the floor and take three slow, deep breaths. Nia copied her with great seriousness, hiccupped twice and announced that she felt a little better. It was a tiny lesson, but Maya understood that she was passing on something that had once been given to her.

That is all the practice asks of you: to be here, to breathe, to notice what is happening without judgment, and to begin again as often as you need. Mindfulness is a skill and a companion, not a cure, and this book offers general information only and cannot replace advice from a professional. If you feel very low or anxious for a long time, please speak to your doctor or someone you trust.
